problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###

**a. Verdict:**  
I have successfully solved the problem. The final answer is \boxed{4048}.

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Permutation of uncovered squares.**  
   Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the uncovered squares form a permutation matrix: there is a permutation \(p\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (\(n=2025\)) such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,p(i))\).

2. **Left and right regions.**  
   For a fixed permutation \(p\) define  
   \[
   L=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le n,\;1\le j<p(i)\},\qquad 
   R=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le n,\;p(i)<j\le n\}.
   \]
   The set of cells to be tiled is \(L\cup R\); a tile cannot contain a hole, hence a tile can intersect only one of the two sets.

3. **Intervals of rows for each column.**  
   For each column \(k\;(1\le k\le n-1)\) put  
   \[
   B_k(i)=\begin{cases}
            1,&p(i)>k,\\[2pt]
            0,&p(i)\le k,
          \end{cases}\qquad i=1,\dots ,n .
   \]
   The rows where column \(k\) belongs to \(L\) are exactly the indices \(i\) with \(B_k(i)=1\).  
   The binary word \(B_k\) splits into a collection of maximal contiguous blocks of 1’s; each block is a **row‑interval** that must be covered by at least one tile (a tile can cover only a contiguous set of rows).  
   Analogously, for the right side define \(C_k(i)=\mathbf 1_{\{p(i)<k\}}\) (\(k=2,\dots ,n\)); its blocks of 1’s are the row‑intervals for column \(k\) in \(R\).

4. **Counting the row‑intervals.**  
   An interval begins exactly when a binary word changes from 0 to 1, or at the first row if the word starts with 1.  
   - For the left side, the number of intervals equals  
     \[
     (p(1)-1)+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\max\bigl(0,\;p(i+1)-p(i)\bigr).
     \tag{1}
     \]
     Indeed, columns \(1,\dots ,p(1)-1\) start a block at row 1, and whenever \(p(i+1)>p(i)\) the columns \(p(i)+1,\dots ,p(i+1)\) start new blocks at row \(i+1\).  
   - For the right side the analogous count is  
     \[
     (n-p(1))+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\max\bigl(0,\;p(i)-p(i+1)\bigr).
     \tag{2}
     \]

   Adding (1) and (2) we obtain the total number of row‑intervals (both sides):
   \[
   \boxed{\,\mathcal I(p)= (n-1)+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\bigl|p(i+1)-p(i)\bigr|\,}.
   \tag{3}
   \]

   Since each interval must be covered by at least one tile, any tiling uses at least \(\mathcal I(p)\) tiles.

5. **A universal lower bound.**  
   For every \(i\) we have \(p(i+1)\neq p(i)\); consequently \(|p(i+1)-p(i)|\ge1\). Hence
   \[
   \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\bigl|p(i+1)-p(i)\bigr|\ge n-1,
   \]
   and from (3)
   \[
   \text{#tiles}\;\ge\;(n-1)+(n-1)=2(n-1).
   \tag{4}
   \]

   Equality in (4) holds precisely when \(|p(i+1)-p(i)|=1\) for all \(i\), i.e. when \(p\) is monotone:
   \[
   p(i)=i\quad\text{or}\quad p(i)=n+1-i\qquad(i=1,\dots ,n).
   \tag{5}
   \]

6. **Construction attaining the bound.**  
   Choose the monotone permutation \(p(i)=i\) (holes on the main diagonal).  
   - For each column \(k=1,\dots ,n-1\) the rows where column \(k\) lies left of the hole are exactly \(i=k+1,\dots ,n\); they form a single interval. Cover this interval by the vertical \(1\times (n-k)\) rectangle  
     \[
     L_k=\{(i,k)\mid i=k+1,\dots ,n\}.
     \]
   - For each column \(k=2,\dots ,n\) the rows where column \(k\) lies right of the hole are \(i=1,\dots ,k-1\); cover them by the vertical rectangle  
     \[
     R_k=\{(i,k)\mid i=1,\dots ,k-1\}.
     \]

   The \(n-1\) rectangles \(\{L_k\}\) are pairwise disjoint and cover all cells of \(L\); the \(n-1\) rectangles \(\{R_k\}\) are disjoint and cover all cells of \(R\). Together they cover every unit square except the diagonal holes, and the total number of tiles is
   \[
   (n-1)+(n-1)=2(n-1).
   \]

   Thus the lower bound (4) is attainable.

7. **Conclusion.**  
   For an \(n\times n\) board the minimal number of tiles equals \(2(n-1)\). With \(n=2025\) we obtain
   \[
   \boxed{2(2025-1)=4048}.
   \]  

### Detailed Solution ###

Let \(n=2025\).  
We work for a general \(n\times n\) board and substitute \(n=2025\) at the end.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.  The uncovered squares form a permutation matrix  

Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, there exists a bijection  

\[
p:\{1,\dots ,n\}\longrightarrow\{1,\dots ,n\}
\]

such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) is the cell \((i,p(i))\).  
Thus the set of uncovered cells is  

\[
U=\{(i,p(i))\mid i=1,\dots ,n\},
\]

and \(p\) is a permutation of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  Left and right regions  

For a row \(i\) the cells **left** of the hole are  

\[
L_i=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le j<p(i)\},
\qquad
\ell_i:=|L_i|=p(i)-1 .
\]

The cells **right** of the hole are  

\[
R_i=\{(i,j)\mid p(i)<j\le n\},
\qquad
r_i:=|R_i|=n-p(i) .
\]

Set  

\[
L=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}L_i,\qquad 
R=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}R_i .
\]

Every admissible tile (axis‑parallel rectangle) cannot contain a hole; consequently a tile intersecting \(L\) is completely contained in \(L\), and similarly for \(R\).  
Hence a tiling of the board consists of a family \(\mathcal L\) of rectangles covering \(L\) and a family \(\mathcal R\) covering \(R\); the two families are disjoint.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  Row‑intervals for a fixed column  

Fix a column \(k\) with \(1\le k\le n-1\).  
Define the binary word  

\[
B_k(i)=\begin{cases}
1,&p(i)>k,\\[2pt]
0,&p(i)\le k,
\end{cases}\qquad i=1,\dots ,n .
\tag{3.1}
\]

Thus \(B_k(i)=1\) exactly when column \(k\) belongs to the left region \(L\) in row \(i\).  
The set \(\{i\mid B_k(i)=1\}\) splits into a collection of maximal contiguous blocks of 1’s; each block is a **row‑interval** of column \(k\) in \(L\).  

A rectangle covering column \(k\) can intersect only one such block, because its rows must form a contiguous interval. Consequently **every block of 1’s in \(B_k\) must be covered by at least one rectangle**.  

Analogously, for the right side we define for \(k=2,\dots ,n\)

\[
C_k(i)=\mathbf 1_{\{p(i)<k\}}=
\begin{cases}
1,&p(i)<k,\\[2pt]
0,&p(i)\ge k,
\end{cases}
\tag{3.2}
\]

and the blocks of 1’s in \(C_k\) are the row‑intervals of column \(k\) in \(R\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.  Counting the row‑intervals  

A block of 1’s begins either at the first row (if the word starts with 1) or at a position where the word changes from 0 to 1.  

*Left side.*  
At row 1 the words \(B_k\) start with 1 precisely for the columns \(k=1,\dots ,p(1)-1\); hence there are \(p(1)-1\) blocks that start at row 1.  

When we pass from row \(i\) to row \(i+1\) (\(1\le i\le n-1\)) the value of \(p\) changes from \(p(i)\) to \(p(i+1)\).  
If \(p(i+1)>p(i)\) then for each column  

\[
k\in\{p(i)+1,\dots ,p(i+1)\}
\]

the word \(B_k\) changes from 0 (at row \(i\)) to 1 (at row \(i+1\)); thus exactly \(\max\bigl(0,\;p(i+1)-p(i)\bigr)\) new blocks start at row \(i+1\).  

Summing over all rows we obtain the total number of left‑side blocks:

\[
\boxed{\; (p(1)-1)+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\max\bigl(0,\;p(i+1)-p(i)\bigr)\; } .
\tag{4.1}
\]

*Right side.*  
The same reasoning applied to the words \(C_k\) yields the total number of right‑side blocks:

\[
\boxed{\; (n-p(1))+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\max\bigl(0,\;p(i)-p(i+1)\bigr)\; } .
\tag{4.2}
\]

*Both sides together.*  
Adding (4.1) and (4.2) gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal I(p)
   &=\bigl(p(1)-1\bigr)+\bigl(n-p(1)\bigr)
     +\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\Bigl(\max\bigl(0,\;p(i+1)-p(i)\bigr)
                           +\max\bigl(0,\;p(i)-p(i+1)\bigr)\Bigr)\\
   &= (n-1)+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\bigl|p(i+1)-p(i)\bigr|.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.3}
\]

The quantity \(\mathcal I(p)\) is precisely the number of distinct row‑intervals that appear in the left or right region.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.  From intervals to a lower bound on the number of tiles  

Each row‑interval must be covered by at least one rectangle, because a rectangle can intersect only a single contiguous block of rows in a given column.  
A rectangle may cover several columns **provided that those columns have exactly the same row‑interval**; nevertheless one rectangle can serve only one interval.  
Hence the total number of tiles is at least the number of distinct intervals:

\[
\boxed{\text{#tiles}\;\ge\;\mathcal I(p)
      =(n-1)+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\bigl|p(i+1)-p(i)\bigr| } .
\tag{5.1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 6.  A universal lower bound  

For a permutation we have \(p(i+1)\neq p(i)\) for every \(i\); therefore \(|p(i+1)-p(i)|\ge1\).  Consequently

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\bigl|p(i+1)-p(i)\bigr|\ge n-1 .
\]

Inserting this into (5.1) yields

\[
\text{#tiles}\;\ge\;(n-1)+(n-1)=2(n-1).
\tag{6.1}
\]

Equality in (6.1) occurs exactly when \(|p(i+1)-p(i)|=1\) for all \(i\), i.e. when the permutation is monotone:

\[
p(i)=i\quad\text{or}\quad p(i)=n+1-i\qquad(i=1,\dots ,n).
\tag{6.2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 7.  Construction attaining the bound  

Assume the monotone permutation \(p(i)=i\) (holes on the main diagonal).  

*Left side.*  
For each column \(k\) with \(1\le k\le n-1\) the rows where column \(k\) lies left of the hole are exactly  

\[
\{\,i\mid i>k\,\}= \{k+1,\dots ,n\},
\]

a single interval.  Cover it by the vertical rectangle  

\[
L_k=\{(i,k)\mid i=k+1,\dots ,n\}.
\]

These \(n-1\) rectangles are pairwise disjoint and together cover the whole set \(L\).

*Right side.*  
For each column \(k\) with \(2\le k\le n\) the rows where column \(k\) lies right of the hole are  

\[
\{\,i\mid i<k\,\}= \{1,\dots ,k-1\},
\]

again a single interval.  Cover it by  

\[
R_k=\{(i,k)\mid i=1,\dots ,k-1\}.
\]

These \(n-1\) rectangles are disjoint from each other and from the rectangles \(L_k\), and they cover the whole set \(R\).

Thus the \(2(n-1)\) rectangles \(\{L_k\}_{k=1}^{n-1}\cup\{R_k\}_{k=2}^{n}\) tile the board, leaving exactly the diagonal cells \((i,i)\) uncovered.  Hence the lower bound (6.1) is attainable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 8.  Final answer  

For the original board \(n=2025\),

\[
\text{minimum number of tiles}=2(2025-1)=\boxed{4048}.
\]
